::::::: {.page-wrap}

::: {.research-lede}
My research concerns discounting, the decrease in the subjective value of delayed and probabilistic outcomes, and its role in decision-making across the adult lifespan.  This research comprises four lines of work, described below with selected publications.
:::

:::::: {.research-area}

::: {.area-head}
[Research area 01]{.area-eyebrow}

## Age-related differences in discounting {#lifespan}

[How does discounting differ with age, and what are the sources of these differences?]{.area-question}
:::

::::: {.grid}

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-7}
There is no consensus as to whether, or in which direction, discounting differs with age, and recent meta-analyses have concluded that adult age differences are small at best.  These analyses, however, did not systematically take socioeconomic status into account.  Our studies of younger and older adults with lower and higher incomes revealed age differences that were modest but systematic: Older adults discounted delayed gains and delayed losses less steeply than younger adults, whereas they discounted probabilistic gains more steeply.  Current research examines the sources of these differences and, in particular, the extent to which they reflect people's financial circumstances.
::::

[Research area 02]{.area-eyebrow}

## Decision-making in more complicated situations {#multiattribute}

[Can decisions in more complicated situations be predicted from simple choices?]{.area-question}
:::

::::: {.grid}

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-7}
Most of what is known about discounting comes from simple choices in which outcomes differ only in amount and in either delay or probability.  Many everyday decisions, however, involve outcomes that are both delayed and probabilistic or that combine gains with losses.  We examine whether decisions in these more complicated situations can be predicted from simple choices.  When rewards were both delayed and probabilistic, delay discounting was much shallower than simple choices would lead one to expect, and none of three prominent models predicted this delay–probability asymmetry.  Current research extends this approach to other kinds of outcomes and to adults of different ages and incomes.
::::

[Research area 03]{.area-eyebrow}

## Measurement of discounting {#measurement}

[Do different procedures and measures assess the same construct?]{.area-question}
:::

::::: {.grid}

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-7}
Conclusions regarding individual and group differences in discounting depend on how discounting is measured.  We examine whether different procedures and different measures of the degree of discounting assess the same construct.  Our studies indicate that they do, both for delayed gains and for delayed losses.  We have also developed brief questionnaires that retain the measurement quality of longer ones and whose brevity lends itself to online surveys with large samples.
::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-5 .selected-works}

[Research area 04]{.area-eyebrow}

## Basic processes of choice {#foundations}

[What principles of choice can be established under controlled laboratory conditions?]{.area-question}
:::

::::: {.grid}

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-7}
Research with animals makes it possible to study choice under conditions that can be controlled more precisely than is usually possible in research with humans.  In collaborative studies with pigeons and rats, we apply the behavioral-economic concepts used to study human decision-making, such as demand and discounting, to choices involving food, tokens, and social interaction.  These studies show that animals' choices are orderly and well described by quantitative models of demand and discounting, providing a controlled setting in which to evaluate behavioral-economic theory.
::::
